data.title: Crude Futures Rise on Persistent Supply Jitters — Market Talk
data.description: The oil market shakes off early lethargy and pushes prices higher as conflict in the Middle East and Ukraine's renewed targeting of Russian refineries fuels supply concerns. "The main source of international uncertainty remains the security of energy transportation in the Middle East," XS.com senior market analyst Antonio Di Giacomo says in a note. "Risks to Russian energy infrastructure add to this backdrop." Front-month WTI settles up 3.5% at $101.41 a barrel, its highest close in a month, while Brent gains 3.7% to $109.86, its highest since May 19. The $100-per-barrel area is a psychological reference for WTI, Di Giacomo says. "Holding above that level would reinforce perceptions of supply pressure, although it would not guarantee further gains." (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

data.title: Oil Futures Rise on Middle East, Russia-Ukraine Concerns — 3rd Update
data.description:
By Farhan Rafid and Anthony Harrup

Oil prices rose Friday after Ukraine renewed attacks on Russian refineries, adding to concerns about persistent Middle East supply risks and uncertainty over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude for December delivery settled up 3.7% at $109.86 a barrel, and December West Texas Intermediate gained 2.6% to $99.02 a barrel. Front-month WTI for November rose 3.5% to $101.41 a barrel, topping the $100 mark for the first time in a month.

"The main reason is that Ukraine has renewed its attacks on Russian oil refineries," said Peter Cardillo, chief market economist at Spartan Capital. "Despite the IEA and its member countries having already released approximately 300 million barrels from emergency oil reserves, with another 100 million barrels likely to be released, prices continue to rise."

The International Energy Agency said Thursday that its members agreed to accelerate the release of around 100 million barrels of previously pledged emergency oil stocks, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel to be released as soon as possible.

About 330 million barrels have already been released, and the agency said total releases would exceed the 400 million barrels initially agreed upon in March, with some members contributing additional volumes.

"We're still in a bull market," said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president of trading at BOK Financial. Flows through the Strait of Hormuz aren't reliable, expectations of Russian diesel coming onto the market aren't being met, and with Ukrainian attacks on refineries "those barrels are going to have trouble getting to the market," he said.

A third factor is that demand destruction "at least in the U.S. is not happening," he added.

Despite recovering Middle East oil flows, uncertainty surrounding the conflict continues to support crude prices, analysts at ING said. The bank said a sustained recovery in shipments through the Strait of Hormuz could gradually reduce the geopolitical risk premium, but a U.S.-Iran agreement would be needed to give markets greater confidence that higher flows could be maintained.

However, oil prices above $100 a barrel appear increasingly stretched relative to market fundamentals, according to Norbert Rucker, head of economics and next generation research at Julius Baer. Middle Eastern exports have largely recovered and global inventories remain comfortable, while geopolitical risk premiums and elevated freight costs could ease, he said.

"The relative calm in oil markets seems untenable, as the gradual recovery in Middle East oil flows has come under pressure of late from a resurgence of attacks on shipping," Barclays analyst Amarpreet Singh said in a note. "What looked like a tail risk scenario a few weeks ago--in which a diplomatic resolution takes us back to pre-war levels of Middle East supply and spare capacity--looks an even more remote possibility at this point," he added.

Shipping risks remain high after two cargo ships sank near the Strait of Hormuz following attacks, The Wall Street Journal reported. U.K. Maritime Trade Operations separately reported Wednesday that two container ships were struck by unidentified projectiles while transiting the waterway.

Risks to shipping have pushed up freight and insurance costs, contributing to the higher price of oil.

War-risk premiums add several million dollars per shipment to the cost of moving oil from Hormuz to somewhere else in the world, said Dennis Marvin, head of marine at insurer MSIG USA.

"It's probably as volatile as it has been, and my answer is it's getting worse," he said, noting the addition of Houthi attacks in the Red Sea and the conflict with Saudi Arabia to the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman. "I can't even perceive when the calm is going to come next. I don't see this changing anytime soon."

Write to Farhan Rafid at farhan.rafid@wsj.com and Anthony Harrup at anthony.harrup@wsj.com

data.title: Fujitsu Japan to offer cloud-native electronic health record system compliant with Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare's standard specifications and certification program
data.description:
KAWASAKI, Japan, Oct 16, 2026 - (JCN Newswire) - Fujitsu Japan Limited today announced that it has commenced specification compliance and functional enhancements for its cloud-native electronic health record (EHR) system [1], currently under development, effective October 16, 2026. This initiative follows the public announcement of the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare's (MHLW) standard specifications and certification program for EHR systems targeting clinics and small to medium-sized hospitals. Fujitsu Japan aims to launch this cloud-native EHR system in April 2027, leveraging digital technology to address regional medical challenges and realize a society where sustainable healthcare is provided.

Clinics and small to medium-sized hospitals, which are vital to regional healthcare, often face numerous concerns when introducing EHR systems. These include selecting a system suitable for their operations, securing initial implementation and operational costs, a shortage of IT personnel, and managing security risks. Fujitsu Japan will address these challenges by developing and providing an easy-to-use and secure cloud-native EHR system. Furthermore, the system is planned to integrate with various national healthcare digital transformation (DX) services, including the electronic prescription service and the electronic health record information sharing service [2].

Through these efforts, Fujitsu Japan aims to contribute to the widespread adoption of cloud-native EHR systems for small to medium-sized hospitals, facilitating patient information sharing, improving operational efficiency, and enhancing medical services in healthcare institutions.

Looking ahead, Fujitsu Japan plans to offer a highly scalable cloud-native EHR system for large hospitals by fiscal year 2028 [3], enabling flexible integration with external services such as AI and other healthcare systems. The system will respond rapidly to regulatory changes and advances in healthcare DX while enabling the continuous delivery of the latest functionality and advanced security measures. The company is currently participating in the Council for the Modernization of Hospital Information Systems, convened and promoted by the Digital Agency and MHLW, and is advancing development in collaboration with the government. As a top vendor holding a 47% market share in the large hospital sector [4] with solutions such as "Fujitsu Healthcare Solution HOPE LifeMark-HX Cloud," Fujitsu Japan will consolidate its expertise. This will accelerate DX in healthcare settings through enhanced cybersecurity, utilization of medical data, and the application of technologies like generative AI, thereby contributing to the realization of a safe, secure, and sustainable healthcare delivery system.

[1] Cloud-native electronic health record (EHR) system:

An EHR system designed and developed to operate on the cloud, maximizing the characteristics and benefits of cloud computing.

[2] Electronic health record information sharing service:

A system planned by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare to enable the sharing of patient electronic health record information among medical institutions and pharmacies nationwide.

[3] Fiscal year 2028:

Fujitsu Japan's fiscal year ends on March 31.

[4] 47% market share in the large hospital sector:

Calculated by Fujitsu Japan based on hospitals with 400 or more beds, as listed in the "Medical Device Systems White Paper 2026: List of Facilities with Hospital Information Systems (HIS)" from the Monthly New Medical Data Book series.

About Fujitsu

Fujitsu's purpose is to make the world more sustainable by building trust in society through innovation. As the digital transformation partner of choice for customers around the globe, our 100,000 employees work to resolve some of the greatest challenges facing humanity. Our range of services and solutions draw on five key technologies: AI, Computing, Networks, Data & Security, and Converging Technologies, which we bring together to deliver sustainability transformation. Fujitsu Limited (TSE:6702) reported consolidated revenues of 3.5 trillion yen (US$23 billion) for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026 and remains the top digital services company in Japan by market share. data.title: ICE review: Canola Weakens on Seasonal Harvest Pressure
data.description:
WINNIPEG, Manitoba--The ICE Futures canola market was weaker on Friday, hitting fresh seven-week lows as steady farmer selling and bearish technical signals weighed on prices.

  • November canola was down by C$2.90 at C$798.80 per ton, with the move below C$800 per ton bearish from a chart standpoint.
  • Losses in the Chicago soy complex and European rapeseed contributed to the softer tone in canola, although Malaysian palm oil was firmer to end the week.
  • Seasonal harvest pressure remained a bearish influence, as warm and dry forecasts across most of the Prairies this weekend should allow farmers to make good progress bringing in the last of the crop.
  • Farmers delivered 620,100 tons of canola into the commercial pipeline during the week ended Oct. 11, reported the Canadian Grain Commission. While that was down by 19% from the previous week, crop-year-to-date deliveries at 4.45 million tons are 28% ahead of last year's pace.
  • Weekly Canadian canola exports at 158,300 tons were down from 248,400 tons the previous week. Crop-year-to-date exports are up 44% on the year at 1.38 million tons through 10 weeks.
  • There were 113,995 contracts traded on Friday, which compares with Thursday when 107,034 contracts changed hands. Spreading accounted for 81,200 of the contracts traded.

data.title: FMC downgraded at Jefferies as 'visibility deteriorates, again' with guidance cut
data.description:
FMC Corp. rebounded 1.7% in Friday's trading after plunging 31% in the previous session when the agricultural chemicals company slashed its Q3 revenue guidance to $65M-$125M, far below consensus estimates, with an adjusted EBITDA loss of $510M-$565M, compared to its previous outlook for positive $120M-$140M.

Following the guidance cut, Jefferies analysts Daniel Rizzo and Charles Boakye downgraded FMC shares to Hold from Buy with a new $5 price target, citing limited visibility, macro headwinds, and persistent pressure from generics.

The current crop protection market remains at a trough, and FMC moved to reduce pricing on a wide range of off-patent crop protection products and simplify its North American pricing strategy, no longer using the high-gross margin, high-rebate model; as a result, the company cut its Q3 revenue and EBITDA projections, Rizzo and Boakye said.

Commodity pricing pressures will likely persist through the 2027 growing seasons, the analysts said, estimating a ~10% pricing decline next year in the core portfolio—offsetting 1%-2% volume growth—with rynaxypyr posing another $100M headwind.

On the positive side, new products including biologicals likely remain on track, and the benefits from the footprint optimization likely will be evident by H2 2027, according to Rizzo and Boakye, adding that Fluindapyr continues to ramp, and Dodhylex and Isoflex are positioned for significant growth beginning in 2028.

data.title: Top global climate science body meet ends without deal on review timeline
data.description:
By Sudarshan Varadhan and Kate Abnett

The meeting of the members of the world's leading authority on climate change ended on Friday without an agreement on a timeline to publish its next review of the latest science on the warming planet, four sources familiar with the matter said.

The meeting of representatives to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change from its 195 member states in Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, this week was seen by many as the last chance to agree publication dates before UN climate talks in November 2028, when governments are due to assess progress toward goals set in the 2015 Paris agreement.

The impasse, which has lasted nearly three years, could leave countries to decide the next phase of action without consensus on critical issues, including the extent to which some global warming might be reversible.

The IPCC did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment.

The dispute reflects deep rifts among wealthy industrialized nations, major emerging economies and poorer nations over how to respond to warming temperatures and how much of that burden should be shouldered by different countries.

The possibility that the IPCC's reports might not be ready in time for the 2028 climate talks has alarmed a coalition of 30 countries, including European, Latin American and small-island states pushing for immediate action.

However, countries including India, Kenya, Saudi Arabia, Russia and China are pressing for more time to prepare the IPCC's next reports to ensure scientists from less-resourced countries can make meaningful contributions.

The IPCC's reviews of the world's existing knowledge on climate change carry weight with governments because they are written by hundreds of international experts and approved by every member state.

Its reports are also used by governments to plan their responses to climate change and have been cited in international court rulings.

The UN Environment Programme has said repeatedly that global efforts to limit warming are falling short and that deeper emissions cuts are needed to avoid more extreme weather and climate-related disasters.

data.title: Court backs EPA giving Oklahoma authority over environmental rules on tribal lands
data.description:
Key points:
  • 10th Circuit says EPA had authority under 2005 law to approve Oklahoma's authority
  • EPA had shifted positions during Trump and Biden administrations
  • Dissent says EPA had discretion to impose at least some protections for tribal interests

By Nate Raymond

A divided federal appeals court on Friday upheld a Trump administration decision to unconditionally grant Oklahoma authority over environmental programs on tribal lands within the state.

A 2-1 panel of the Denver-based 10th US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the US Environmental Protection Agency acted in accordance with a long-dormant provision in a 2005 transportation funding bill that allows Oklahoma to seek authority over environmental regulatory programs in Native American territory.

The provision was dubbed the "Midnight Rider" because it was added late and without discussion to the Safe, Accountable, Flexible, Efficient Transportation Equity Act.

Oklahoma did not invoke the provision until 2020, after the US Supreme Court's 5-4 decision in McGirt v. Oklahoma, which recognized about half of Oklahoma — much of the eastern part of the state — as Native American reservation land beyond the jurisdiction of state authorities.

Later that year, the EPA during President Donald Trump’s first administration approved Oklahoma’s request.

At the request of several tribes including the Pawnee Nation, the EPA under Democratic President Joe Biden withdrew the approval in 2021 and reconsidered the matter. In Biden's final days in office, the EPA again approved Oklahoma's request but with a condition that the state engage in efforts to seek consensus with affected tribes.

But once Trump returned to the White House, the agency issued a new decision last year eliminating that condition, prompting a lawsuit by the Pawnee Nation.

The tribe argued the EPA’s action violated the Administrative Procedure Act, saying the Midnight Rider expired in 2009 along with other parts of the 2005 spending law and that EPA wrongly under Trump concluded it had no authority to impose conditions when approving Oklahoma's request.

But US Circuit Judge Timothy Tymkovich, writing for the majority, said the Midnight Rider contained no sunset provision and did not authorize the Biden-era condition.

"Congress’s command that the EPA 'shall approve' a valid request does not authorize the agency to shrink that approval by attaching a condition to it," he wrote.

Michael Freedman, a lawyer for Pawnee Nation at Earthjustice, did not respond to a request for comment.

Tymkovich, who was appointed by Republican President George W. Bush, was joined by US Circuit Judge Robert Bacharach, an appointee of Democratic President Barack Obama.

US Circuit Judge Richard Federico, a Biden appointee, dissented, saying the EPA had the discretion to impose at least some protections for tribal interests.

"This court should not so readily acquiesce to the total displacement of the tribes as the first sovereigns of their land absent a clear statement from Congress to the contrary," he wrote.

The case is Pawnee Nation of Oklahoma v Zeldin, 10th US Circuit Court of Appeals, No. 25-9548.

For Pawnee Nation of Oklahoma: Michael Freedman of Earthjustice

For the United States: Cameron Hinojos of the US Department of Justice

EPA withdraws Trump Oklahoma environment order after input from tribes

Tribes slam EPA move to give Oklahoma control of environmental rules

data.title: U.S. Natural Gas Futures Settle Lower — Market Talk
data.description: U.S. natural gas futures fall as the market looks beyond this weekend's cold spell in the Northeast that is expected to drive up residential and commercial heating demand. "Heating demand should retreat after the weekend, but supply restrictions could persist longer, while firm LNG utilization continues to cushion the decline in domestic consumption," Gelber & Associates says in a note. "Traders may also be reassessing Thursday's 67 Bcf [storage] injection: the smaller build initially attracted buying, but inventories remain above the five-year average, El Niño-related expectations continue to temper the winter demand outlook." Nymex natural gas settles down 3.7% at $3.116/mmBtu. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

data.title: Bitcoin Closes Week Sliding After Attempted Rally
data.description:
By Kirk Maltais

Bitcoin turned lower in late morning trade, retesting the $80,000 threshold heading into the weekend.

The flagship cryptocurrency is down 1.3% to $80,970 Friday afternoon, according to pricing data from LSEG. The cryptocurrency had rallied along with the stock markets in morning trade, but succumbed to continued weakness seen in tech and AI stocks, following the 2.4% slide seen on the Nasdaq.

Bond yields turned higher in the afternoon, this after the Treasury Department passed on an opportunity to send a strong signal that it is considering reducing the sizes of bond auctions. Higher yields have been a pressure point for cryptocurrencies and general commodities, with investors cautious about engaging with what they perceive as "riskier" assets.

Crypto assets were supported in morning trade by dimming expectations for a near-term Federal Reserve rate hike. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh avoided a clearly hawkish or dovish tone during a moderated conversation at the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok.

But for bitcoin, lacking demand for tokens on the spot market is a fundamental problem that hasn't gone away.

"The demand picture has not improved," said Colin Basco, a senior quantitative analyst with Coinbase Institutional. Basco attributes the upward movement seen in bitcoin earlier in the week to trading by leveraged long positions, as opposed to spot demand among investors.

Net flows in and out of bitcoin ETFs, considered a metric of interest in the cryptocurrency among fund managers, have slid back into being more negative than positive for the week. Through Thursday, bitcoin ETFs recorded a net outflow of $146 million, according to data from Coinglass.

At the same time, analysts say that bitcoin's relative strength versus AI stocks this week is reason for optimism. Bitcoin shed roughly 3% this week, while the iShares Semiconductor ETF slipped 9%.

Write to Kirk Maltais at kirk.maltais@wsj.com

data.title: Atlantic American Extends Reporting Deadlines Under Truist Credit Facility; Sets A- Rating Covenant
data.description:

A Fourth Amendment signed October 9, 2026 extends the delivery dates for 2025 audited financials to October 15, 2026 and 2026 interim financials to November 30, 2026, along with related compliance certificates. A Fifth Amendment and Waiver signed October 15, 2026 further extends the 2025 audit delivery and certificates to October 23, 2026, establishes a minimum AM Best financial strength rating of A- for American Southern Insurance Company, and waives related prior defaults. data.title: Moderna and Novavax Stocks Slump as Biotech's Rally Takes a Breather — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Mackenzie Tatananni

Biotechnology stocks slumped Friday, led by high-flying vaccine makers and drug developers.

Moderna was falling particularly hard. That is nothing new for the stock, which has risen more than sevenfold this year, fueled by a cancer vaccine trial readout in August that launched shares into the stratosphere.

Since then, shares have been volatile. Moderna fell 9.3% to $214.60 on Friday to become one of the worst-performing stocks in the S&P 500.

Novavax fared even worse, plunging 12%. Broad selling pressure across vaccine stocks hit the company hard, amplified by a bearish note from Citi analyst Geoff Meacham late Thursday. Reiterating his Sell rating on the shares, Meacham noted that "timing, economics, and long-term revenue visibility remain difficult to underwrite."

Beyond vaccine stocks, biotech more broadly was falling. The iShares Biotechnology exchange-traded fund, which counts Amgen and Moderna among its largest holdings, was down 1.8% on Friday. Another major holding, cancer-drug developer Revolution Medicines, fell 5.9%.

One down session doesn't necessarily signal the end of the rally. While several biotech high-flyers have enjoyed a banner year — with Novavax up 67%, Revolution Medicines up 124%, and Moderna up an eye-watering 622% — a single day in the red doesn't necessarily mean the gains are over.

Several closely watched companies face near-term catalysts in the coming weeks. Moderna, for instance, is slated to present three abstracts on intismeran autogene — its personalized cancer vaccine co-developed with Merck — at an oncology conference later this month.

The presentations include expanded results from the Phase 3 trial previewed in August, which assessed a combination of intismeran autogene and Merck's Keytruda as an adjuvant treatment for resected melanoma. Goldman Sachs analyst Salveen Richter characterized these results as "the initial unlock for Moderna's cancer vertical," noting that they marked the company's first positive pivotal data outside its respiratory vaccine franchise.

Indeed, the data appear to have fundamentally reframed Moderna's identity, showing its pipeline extends far beyond Covid-19 and demonstrating the versatility of its core mRNA platform.

Speaking at the 2026 STAT Summit on Thursday, Moderna President Stephen Hoge recalled that intismeran faced deep skepticism early on. "We believed in it, but going into it, you'd have to describe it as a risky bet," Hoge said. "It was a long shot by any stretch of the imagination in the early days."

Revolution Medicines, too, may still have room to run following an impressive rally this year. Shares had a surprisingly muted reaction to the U.S. approval of Rasonque, despite months of buildup surrounding the pancreatic cancer therapy, which drew a minute-long standing ovation at a medical conference ahead of its authorization.

However, a major second market could soon open up. On Thursday, a European Medicines Agency committee recommended granting Rasonque marketing authorization in the European Union, a critical step toward bringing a new option to patients with a notoriously hard-to-treat disease.

With the European Commission facing a 67-day deadline to issue a final verdict, investors now have a clear timeline for the drug's next catalyst. A similar countdown is underway for Eli Lilly, which awaits a decision on marketing authorization for its weight-loss pill, Foundayo.

The road ahead may be tougher for companies like Novavax, which have more to prove, for many other biotechs, a single red day is far from the end of the story.

Write to Mackenzie Tatananni at mackenzie.tatananni@barrons.com

data.title: Stocks slip as dollar heads for weekly loss
data.description:
Key points:
  • US dollar heads for weekly loss on lower US Treasury yields
  • Bond markets stabilise after rush for safe havens on Thursday
  • Investors worry about debt risks in AI-related stocks

By Chibuike Oguh and Elizabeth Howcroft

Global stocks fell modestly on Friday as markets stabilised after a sharp tech-led selloff, while the dollar headed for a weekly loss.

Markets have been rattled this week by concerns over higher interest rates and the debt-fuelled financing behind the AI boom, triggering a selloff in technology and chip stocks.

Traders increased bets on further US rate hikes after stronger-than-expected inflation data was released on Wednesday, while investors piled into Treasuries and other government bonds.

On Wall Street, the benchmark S&P 500 and the Nasdaq were trading down and were headed for weekly losses. The Dow was lower after reversing early gains but was still set for a weekly gain.

Technology and communication services were driving losses while the top gainers were utilities and energy stocks.

CoreWeave's shares shed 13% and were on track to lose nearly 26% this week amid increasing investor scrutiny of the financing for the massive AI infrastructure buildout.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.57%, the S&P 500 CBOE:SPX lost 1.3%, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.3%.

The MSCI World Equity Index lost 0.54% and was set for a weekly loss EURONEXT:IACWI. European stock indexes, hit less hard by Thursday's selloff, gained, with the STOXX 600 adding 0.72% . London's FTSE 100 CURRENCYCOM:UK100 rose 0.38%.

"We're starting to see some cracks in the financing of data centers because you're not too sure who's going to be the winners," said Tom Plumb, portfolio manager at Plumb Balanced Fund.

"Our view is that there's going to be some really significant winners. But you have to be careful on the financing capability because companies don't get into trouble because their assets don't exceed their liabilities. They get into trouble when they have liquidity issues."

Asian stocks mostly rose, and bond markets steadied, with investors reversing some of the previous session's moves.

Indonesian equities suffered their biggest drop since 1998 after index provider MSCI said the country's market no longer merited emerging-market status and outlined plans to remove it from key indexes tracked by funds.

DOLLAR FALLS, BONDS RECOVER

The dollar index fell 0.21% and was on track for its first weekly decline after four weeks of gains, as lower Treasury yields reduced the currency's appeal. Further worries about AI would push the dollar down further, analysts said.

The euro rose from its recent 17-month low. It was last up 0.1% at $1.12315 .

The Japanese yen weakened 0.03% against the greenback to 158.05 per dollar.

European government bond yields edged higher, while US bond yields reversed earlier declines. Germany's 10-year yield rose 4.36 basis points to 3.453% (DE10YT=RR). The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes rose 2.13 basis points to 5.108%.

Even so, yields have eased this week as investors sought the safety of government debt amid concerns about AI-related companies' finances. G7 government bond markets were on course for their strongest weekly performance since late May.

Brent crude futures rose 3.72% to settle at $109.86 a barrel and were headed for a second straight weekly gain amid concerns over Middle East supplies. Attacks around the Strait of Hormuz have surged in the past 10 days.

Gold (XAU) gained support from the weaker dollar, rising 0.25% to $4,159.69 an ounce.

data.title: Cleveland-Cliffs Braces for Fight as Canada Looks to Block Layoffs at Stelco — Interview
data.description:
(19:37 GMT) *Canadian Govt Says Cleveland-Cliffs Must Abide by Commitments to Maintain Stelco Jobs
(19:37 GMT) *Canada Industry Minister Says Govt Looking at All Options to Protect Stelco Jobs
(19:37 GMT) *Canada Industry Minister: Cleveland-Cliffs Could Be Forced to Sell Canadian Assets if Commitments Not Kept
(19:37 GMT) *Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Says No Laws Broken With Planned Stelco Layoffs
(19:37 GMT) *Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Says Tariffs Putting Pressure on Galvanized Steel Market
(19:37 GMT) *Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Says Stelco Business Remains Strong, Focusing on Hot-Roll Production
(19:37 GMT) Cleveland-Cliffs Braces for Fight as Canada Looks to Block Layoffs at Stelco — Interview

By Robb M. Stewart

OTTAWA--Cleveland-Cliffs is digging in on planned lay offs at its Stelco operations in Canada as Prime Minister Mark Carney's government weighs legal options, including fines and potentially forced sale of assets, to protect workers.

Calls for Ottawa to take action have grown in recent days after Stelco began handing out layoff notices. Industry Minister Melanie Joly had earlier requested that the steel company produce a plan to comply with promises on jobs she said were agreed to when Cliffs bought Stelco in 2024 for about $2.5 billion.

Cliffs Chief Executive Lourenco Goncalves said the company hasn't breached the law and that a temporary reduction in headcount is needed as it refocuses its operations to counter the pressure on the industry from tariffs. The company, which is set to report quarterly results on Monday, said it could lay off as many as 500 workers as it idles cold-rolled and coated steel operations in Hamilton, Ontario, and concentrates on hot-roll products.

"For the time being, employees that are employed to produce galvanized steel need to be laid off until we have a market for galvanized steel again," Goncalves said in an interview. "I don't know when, because I'm not the government of Canada and I'm not the government of the United States."

Goncalves said he has been made to feel like an enemy in Canada because of his support for President Trump's tariffs. He added that the blame for the latest stresses on the steel industry in the country lies with Carney and his decision to walk away from trade negotiations in August that were aimed at staving off fresh U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods.

"I believed in the country. I believed in the workforce. I believed in the Canadian market," he said. "I paid 3.4 billion Canadian dollars for the company, not to be treated less than two years after the acquisition, after all the charming, all the dinners, [as] enemy number one."

Minister Joly described what is happening at Stelco is unacceptable.

"Cleveland-Cliffs came to Canada back in the day to be part of the solution and now they have spoken in favor of U.S. tariffs, ones that are directly harming Stelco's own business right here at home and putting hundreds of jobs at risk," Joly said Friday at an event in Toronto. "They must keep the jobs in Canada or face the prospect of having to sell their Canadian assets."

Under the Investment Canada Act, the government's options in court include seeking financial penalties, forcing the company to abide by commitments and a forced divestiture of the Canadian assets. Joly has said that Cliffs, as part of securing government approval for its takeover of Stelco, pledged to maintain the same number of unionized employees at the Canadian operations for five years and honor collective bargaining agreements.

The United Steelworkers union said that although it recognizes the stresses on Canada's steel industry, difficult market conditions can't automatically erase commitments that were central to the approval of a major foreign acquisition.

Opposition lawmakers are pushing the Liberal government to act quickly.

Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre has said the government should sue Stelco and obtain court orders against its parent company, which if needed could include an order to sell Stelco to a Canadian buyer. The left-leaning New Democratic Party argued the country can't afford to lose its steel industry and that Carney should nationalize Stelco.

A normal trade environment between Canada and the U.S. doesn't exist as it stands, Goncalves said. "We are not part of the negotiation between the U.S. and Canada," he said. "We can influence, we can express our opinion, but we are not at that table."

Goncalves said he was forced to issue the layoff notices because of Canada's lack of support for the galvanized steel market which, in addition to tariffs, faces pressure from lower-price imports. He said Stelco President Paul Simon wrote to Joly to convey that conditions were getting worse and that the company would have to concentrate on hot-roll production. He added that Stelco overall remains strong and is producing more steel, which means 2,150 jobs are safe.

The United Steelworkers union in Canada said there have been two rounds of layoffs in Hamilton to date, though none at Stelco's Lake Erie operation in Nanticoke, Ontario, where it expects 40 positions to be targeted.

Guio Jacinto, head of the union's research department in Toronto, said the current dispute at Stelco adds to the company's troubled history. During a period of steel market consolidation in the mid to late 2000s, Stelco was bought by US Steel, which shuttered Canadian capacity and reduced operations in the country, diverting U.S. sales to U.S.-based capacity, he said.

Cliffs picked up the company from American Alan Kestenbaum, who from 2017 helped turn the business around. But Jacinto said Stelco is again idling Canadian capacity, removing Stelco supply from the U.S. and diverting production.
